listings.description:
In 2025, Americans spent more than 400 billion hours inside work organizations. Nir Halevy's argument is that what happens in those hours, how people are ranked, rewarded, promoted, and treated, is one of the most consequential ways corporations shape society, even when it never reaches the headlines. Drawing on his new book Level Up: Why Hierarchies Are Broken and How to Fix Them, Halevy explains why hierarchies break, why the damage lands first on employees and then on customers, communities, and the public, and what it would take to repair them.

Nir Halevy is the Jagdeep and Roshni Singh Professor of Organizational Behavior at the Stanford Graduate School of Business and the author of Level Up: Why Hierarchies Are Broken and How to Fix Them. An expert in organizational hierarchy, power, status, leadership, negotiation, conflict management, and cooperation, Halevy examines how individuals and groups make decisions, exercise influence, compete, collaborate, and resolve conflict. He has taught courses and executive workshops at Stanford GSB since 2010. His research has appeared in leading academic journals and has been featured by The Economist, The Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, Forbes, Businessweek, CNN, and MSNBC. He holds a PhD in Social Psychology and Management, an MA in Social and Organizational Psychology, and a BA in Psychology and International Relations from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

listings.title: Alain Schläpfer — Why Do Voters Elect Authoritarians? How Scandal Signals Independence from Elites
listings.description:
Politicians who openly display anti-democratic traits can attract substantial electoral support, even among voters who value democracy. This paper argues that the very behavior that makes a politician objectionable can also reassure voters that the politician will remain independent of political elites. Voters whose preferred policies lie far from elite interests worry that the candidates they elect will be captured by elites once in office. Because capturing a politician mired in scandal is costly for elites, scandalous behavior can credibly signal that a candidate is beyond elite reach. Where elites are democratically committed, displays of anti-democratic intent become an efficient way to generate such a scandal. Voters may elect these candidates even though they are more likely to manipulate elections once in office, an outcome costly for voters and elites alike. Elites who can perfectly anticipate which politicians will subvert elections have no credible way to communicate this to voters. A reanalysis of existing experimental data is consistent with the model's central prediction. Unlike existing accounts of anti-democratic voting, this theory explains why citizens who value democracy may still elect an anti-democratic candidate, even when a democratically committed candidate offers the same policy platform.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER

Alain Schläpfer is a social science research scholar at Stanford University’s Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL), and a lecturer in Stanford’s Ford Dorsey Master’s in International Policy. His research lies at the intersection of political science and economics and focuses on cooperation, political institutions, and intergroup relations. His current work examines how cooperation can be sustained across political and social divisions, why voters support anti-democratic politicians, and how institutions and social norms shape political behavior. His research combines formal theory with experiments and observational data. He holds a PhD in Economics.

Roland Greene, the director of the Stanford Humanities Center, will discuss some of the complexity with which the idea was endowed in antiquity, how early moderns such as Shakespeare and Montaigne reimagined it for their times, and how in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries it has been rethought again. The Night Before series brings you familiar occasions seen in a new light—and what is more familiar than coming home? A light reception will follow immediately after this talk.

listings.description:
Expanding upon the work begun in What Tech Calls Thinking, Adrian Daub explores which ideas of politics, power, and dominance characterize the tech industry, and how those ideas came to be.

Tech companies increasingly determine who regulates and who governs. And the tech elite increasingly wield political power, seeking to remake your workplace, your child's school, and the federal government in their image. But what do they mean by power?

Taking readers from investor meetings to lecture halls, from science fiction to a neo-feudal worldview, Daub acerbically explores how tech culture approaches hierarchy and dominance, and what role a very specific form of masculinity plays in tech culture's ethos. From billboards to social media, Daub interrogates the way the tech elite exert power in their families and offices, but also in gyms and on YouTube channels, in courtrooms and on their commutes. As What Tech Calls Governing shows, to ask "how do they seek to dominate?" is actually to retell the history of Silicon Valley as the story of a fragile—and precisely for that reason domineering—masculinity intent on all the influence with none of the responsibility.

Adrian Daub is J.E. Wallace Sterling Professor in the Humanities at Stanford University, where he serves as the Faculty Director of the Clayman Institute for Gender Research. He is the author of What Tech Calls Thinking (2020) and The Cancel Culture Panic (2024), and writes for numerous US and European newspapers and magazines.

listings.description:
Made possible by the J. Fred Weintz and Rosemary Weintz Art Lecture Series Fund, this series invites distinguished art historians from diverse concentrations each quarter to speak and engage with our students and the Stanford community, enriching the culture of art history and appreciation on campus and beyond.

Marketing Late Antique Textile “Collages”

Hundreds of thousands of late antique Egyptian textiles are preserved in museum collections around the globe, many the result of what would today be considered illicit excavations in the late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century. It is precisely because of their vast numbers and low valuations as individual works that such textiles are rarely assessed as fakes. Yet a group of fabrics depicting dark-skinned figures in racialized terms raises questions about the production of imitation Egyptian textiles for the modern art market and these objects’ lasting reverberations in collections, in exhibitions, and on the art market through the twentieth-century until today. Bringing together close technical analyses, archival research into the objects’ provenance history, and consideration of comparable visual sources, this paper situates non-authentic works as primary sources in the reception history and the historiography of Coptic and Byzantine art.

Biography

Elizabeth Dospěl Williams is Penny Vinik Chair of Fashion, Textiles and Jewelry at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, responsible for global collections from ancient to contemporary. She was previously Curator of the Byzantine Collection at Dumbarton Oaks Research Library and Collection in Washington, D.C., where curated special exhibitions including Rich in Blessings: Women, Wealth, and the Late Antique Household (2023) and Woven Interiors: Furnishing Early Medieval Egypt (2019).

Dospěl Williams has authored numerous chapters and exhibition catalogue essays, with a focus on wearable arts, interior design, provenance history, and comparative art historical approaches. Her research is forthcoming or has appeared in Speculum, West 86th: A Journal of Decorative Arts, Design History, and Material Culture, Dumbarton Oaks Papers, and The Textile Museum Journal. With Eiren Shea and Patricia Blessing, she recently co-authored Medieval Textiles across Eurasia, c. 300-1500 for the Cambridge Elements in the Global Middle Ages Series (2023). Dospěl Williams holds a Ph.D. in Byzantine and Islamic art history and archaeology from the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University.

listings.title: Emily Jacobs - New frontiers in women's brain health
listings.description:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
New frontiers in women's brain health
Abstract
Gonadal hormones are potent neuromodulators of learning and memory. Yet, how these tiny molecules shape the structural and functional architecture of the human brain is virtually unknown. Many brain imaging studies miss a central feature of the endocrine system: hormone production ebbs and flows over time. Precision imaging allows us to map the mammalian brain with exquisite temporal resolution. Following individuals across major endocrine transitions, like the circadian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy, these studies reveal the human brain's capacity for rapid reorganization and hormones' role in shaping this process.
Jacobs' talk also considers why women’s health research is decades behind where it should be. Nowhere is this knowledge gap more visible than in neuroscience, where fewer than 0.5% of brain imaging articles focus on female-specific experiences, including menstruation, pregnancy, and menopause, that shape the lives of half the global population (Jacobs Nature 2023). Progress in women’s health will require a global shift in science culture, and that shift has started. Jacobs will examine emerging research programs, public policy changes, and private sector funding opportunities that are shining a floodlight on women’s health, and by doing so are opening up new frontiers for understanding health and disease.

Emily Jacobs, PhD
Professor Jacobs, University of California, Santa Barbara
Emily Jacobs is a Professor of Neuroscience at UC Santa Barbara and Director of the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative. Her body of research examines dynamic endocrine modulation of the nervous system. In 2024 her team published the first detailed view of the human brain across pregnancy and she leads several multi-center studies on neurological changes tied to menopause. Prior to UCSB, she held a faculty appointment at Harvard Medical School and the Department of Medicine/Division of Women's Health at Brigham & Women's Hospital. She serves on the Steering Committee of the Coalition for Women’s Brain Health, the Milken Institute’s Women’s Health Network, the Foundation for Women’s Health, and the WHAM Research Collaborative to drive the national and international agenda on women’s health research. In recognition of her work, she was named a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Health and Society Scholar, a National Institutes of Health Women's Health Fellow, a National Academy of Sciences Frontiers of Science Kavli Fellow and Science News’ “Top 10 Scientists” to watch. Outside of the lab, Dr. Jacobs’ team partners with K-12 groups to advance girls' representation in STEM. You can find her work in the The New York Times, National Geographic, Scientific American, NPR, BBC, TED, Radiolab, Netflix, and MasterClass. She is a graduate of Smith and UC Berkeley.

listings.description:
Please join the Silicon Valley Archives in welcoming Kimberley Johnson and Pedro Regalado as they discuss Johnson's latest book, Dark Concrete: Black Power, Urbanism, and the American Metropolis, on October 22, 2026, at 4:30 p.m. This event is co-sponsored with the Silicon Valley Archives by the Program on Urban Studies at Stanford, the Stanford Department of African and African American Studies, the Stanford Program in American Studies, and the Stanford Center for Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity.

Please RSVP at this link to attend.

Dark Concrete is about how the Black Power movement reshaped urban politics in the United States—from expectations to practices. Although the national and international dimensions of the Black Power movement are often focused on, Kimberley Johnson looks at the movement at the local level, highlighting Newark and East Orange, New Jersey, and Oakland and East Palo Alto, California, and three policy areas: housing, education, and policing. She examines how Black Power Urbanism had its own local meanings as it was defined by local activists, neighborhood residents, parents, tenants, and others who sought to repair cities and particularly black neighborhoods that were shattered due to urban renewal and highway construction, as well as ongoing political and economic disinvestment. Dark Concrete depicts how local conditions influenced the emergence of the Black Power movement and, in turn, the ways in which these local movements reshaped urban politics, institutions, and place.

Kimberley S. Johnson is Professor of Social and Cultural Analysis at New York University, with affiliate appointments in the Department of Politics and the Wagner Graduate School of Public Service. Johnson recently held the John G. Winant Visiting Professorship in American Government at the University of Oxford (2024-25). Johnson’s work examines American political development, the formation of the modern administrative state and bureaucratic governance; urban and suburban governance; race and ethnic politics; and the political production of (sub-)urban space.

Pedro A. Regalado is an Assistant Professor of History at Stanford University. Regalado's work focuses on cities, immigration, capitalism, and empire, with particular attention to Latino communities. He is especially interested in how everyday working people, migrants, and entrepreneurs shaped, and were shaped by, the political economy of urban America across the twentieth century.

We are excited to celebrate the publication of a new book by our visiting postdoctoral scholar, Danny Shanhan titled, Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland.

This book is the first substantial study of emergency law's relationship to literature in either the Northern Irish or the Kashmiri conflict and develops an original legal history that links these laws to a shared British colonial root. Engaging a wide range of fiction, poetry and film, from canonical poets Seamus Heaney and Agha Shahid Ali to contemporary works by Anna Burns, Mirza Waheed, and Bollywood filmmaker Vishal Bhardwaj, the book examines the literary response to the suspension of normative legal rights such as habeas corpus, the right to silence and even, in Kashmir, the right to life. By bringing these literary cultures together for the first time, it develops a literary and legal history that reveals common roots in colonial-era jurisprudence. The book re-situates these corpora, often isolated in scholarly work, as important parts of the global, material legacies of colonialism.

listings.title: Sociology Lecture Series | The Evolution of Federally-Insured Redlining, 1935-1975
listings.description:
Please join us for this lecture by Jacob W. Faber, part of the Open and Engaged Lecture Series organized by the Department of Sociology.

We introduce a novel dataset describing neighborhood patterns of federally-insured mortgages from 1935 to 1975, the period in which the American homeownership society emerged alongside the exclusion of people and communities of color from mortgage finance through the process of "redlining." Specifically, we collected, digitized, and geocoded over 110,000 home loans insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) or the Veterans Administration (VA). We show both FHA and VA disproportionately insured loans in white, high income, and suburban neighborhoods, though the pattern reversed by 1970 after Civil Rights legislation prohibited explicit racial discrimination. We also describe a typology of Black neighborhoods where FHA/VA loans were made during the earlier period of exclusion.

listings.description:
Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools.

Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other. This exhibition inhabits that intersection, where historic technologies of encoding meet their digital descendants. Printmaking and weaving become contact zones between traditional craft techniques and computational processes, recording and recoding gestures across media: photographs compressed and reassembled as strips, atomized prints woven into textile, and thrown clay fused with digitally printed forms.

Where does resistance live in a material, and how do we encounter it? How do different materials choreograph their maker’s creative gestures through this resistance? As creative workflows migrate into digital space, something of that friction transforms. Tangling the Digital asks what becomes possible when that resistance is embraced rather than engineered away.

A working loom lives in the gallery, bearing witness to the evolution of craft as weavings unfurl over the course of the exhibition.

Together, the works invite visitors to locate the human body—as maker, as observer—in what they see.

In this lecture, authors Aldo Marchesi y Vania Markarian will present their book El tiempo no para. The book aims to trace the history of the idea of human rights and to understand the impact of that concept on the development of democracies at the close of the 20th century and in progressive governments of the 21st century. It further puts forth questions on the limits of the language of human rights when considering the contemporary crisis.

Aldo Marchesi holds a PhD in History from New York University and is a Professor in the Department of Theory and Historiography at the Institute for History at The University of the Republic, as well as a member of the Center for Uruguayan Interdisciplinary Studies. Together with colleagues from other disciplines, he recently founded the Institute for Research on Social Justice and Inequality. He is a member of the National System of Researchers in Uruguay. He has served as a visiting professor at universities and research centers in the United States, Chile, Argentina, Colombia, and China. His work has focused on the recent history of Uruguay and the Southern Cone. He has published numerous articles and books. His first book, reissued in 2023, was El Uruguay Inventado: La política audiovisual durante la dictadura. His most recent book, a regional history of the armed Left in the Southern Cone, was published in Spanish and English under the title Hacer la revolución (Making the Revolution). In 2021 he co-authored, with Vania Markarian and Gerardo Caetano, a book on the Left for the collection Historia de los partidos políticos en Uruguay. He has continued researching the Latin American Left in the 20th century and, within a broader context, Uruguay’s recent history. Since 2023, he has co-directed, together with Diego Sempol, a Research Group on the Left. In 2025, he published El tiempo no para: Historia, crisis y futuro para pensar proyectos de izquierda with Vania Markarian. He is currently completing Una historia mínima de las izquierdas latinoamericanas for El Colegio de México. Professor Marchesi has edited and co-edited several volumes and currently serves on the editorial boards of the journals Contemporánea and The Global Sixties. His current research project is Una Historia intellectual y politics de la idea de pobreza en el Uruguay contemporáneo (1943–2010). As part of this project, he was a research member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. This fall, he is a Tinker Visiting Professor at the Teresa Lozano Long Institute of Latin American Studies at the University of Texas at Austin.

Vania Markarian is the Coordinator of the General Archive at the University of the Republic (Udelar), a full-time tenured professor at the same institution, and a member of the National System of Researchers. She holds a PhD in History from Columbia University and a degree in Historical Sciences from Udelar. She has served as a visiting professor and researcher at various universities in Latin America (such as UNGS, UNSAM, and UFMG) and the United States (including Columbia University, the City University of New York, and Princeton University), as well as at the Sorbonne Nouvelle and the École des hautes études en sciences sociales in France. From 2019 to 2021, she served as President of the Uruguayan Association of Historians. She has published books and articles on her areas of expertise both in Uruguay and abroad. Her main works include Idos y recién llegados: La izquierda uruguaya en el exilio y las redes transnacionales de derechos humanos (1967-1984)—originally published by Routledge as Left in Transformation: Uruguayan Exiles and the Latin American Human Rights Networks—and El 68 uruguayo: El movimiento estudiantil entre molotovs y música beat, which was also published in English by the University of California Press. Her most recent book is Universidad, revolución y dólares: Dos estudios sobre la Guerra Fría cultural en el Uruguay de los sesenta (2020). In 2025, she co-authored El tiempo no para: Historia, crisis y utopía para pensar proyectos de izquierda with Aldo Marchesi.

Socialist Yugoslavia produced two internationally renowned schools of philosophy in the period following the Second World War: the Praxis school in the 1970s and the Ljubljana School in the 1980s, which is today recognized as one of the most important schools of continental philosophy in the world. The lecture will focus on the relationship between, and the conceptual differences separating, the two schools, placing particular emphasis on the figure of Zagorka Golubović, the only woman among the members of Praxis. After losing her position at the University of Belgrade on account of her “dissidence,” Golubović spent some time working in the United States at the invitation of Richard Bernstein. In this context, the lecture will explore the connection between Yugoslavia’s original socio-economic model of self-management and the principle of alienation as a constitutive principle of thought.

listings.description:
Each quarter, the Stanford Archaeology Center invites prominent archaeologists from around the globe to be in residence for a week as a Distinguished Lecturer. During their residency, the Distinguished Lecturer gives two lectures and interacts with faculty, postdoctoral scholars and students. Stanford Archaeology Center will host Prof. Xiaoyan Yang Lanzhou University over two days (Oct 7 and Oct 8 for the Fall Quarter of this academic year.

Abstract:

Sedentism is one of the milestone events in the development of human society. Settlement in ultra-high-altitude regions reflects human physiological and cultural adaptation to extreme environments. Through morphological identification, isotopic analysis, and ancient DNA analysis of faunal and floral remains from the Lapo site (2800 m a.s.l., 4800 BP) and the Mabu Co site (4420–4460 m a.s.l., 4400 BP) on the Tibetan Plateau, we discovered that the process of sedentism on the plateau followed at least two distinct modes. In relatively low-altitude river valleys, intensive millet pig agriculture supported early settlement, whereas in high-altitude regions where crop cultivation is not possible, a fishing hunting economy centered on lake resources initiated the sedentism process.

Koyré, discovering that Galileo and Descartes both moved in parallel towards the discovery of the law of free fall – but that only Galileo made it – used this to identify Galileo’s originality as the first to form the specifically dynamic concepts of modern physics. The more recent realization - that Thomas Harriot, too, made the same discovery as Galileo, following a similar path, and a similarly protracted campaign – should help us see the historical originality not in terms of shared concepts, but instead of shared practices. Tactile Braille Periodic Table: Short History and Evolution

The Tactile Braille Periodic Table at Stanford is part of a broader effort by the American Chemical Society’s Committee on Chemists with Disabilities (ACS CWD) to increase awareness of accessibility and the different ways people experience and access scientific information.

The project traces its roots to an accessible periodic table developed by ACS CWD in 2019, the 150th anniversary of the periodic table. This first-generation table incorporated Braille and American Sign Language into 3D-printed element tiles and served to initiate conversations about disability and accessibility in chemistry. [1,2]

A next-generation tactile periodic table emerged through the work of ACS CWD members Dr. Michael Fricke and Dr. Mona Minkara. Their collaboration resulted in a scalable wooden tactile table designed around Braille, which they described in Nature Reviews Chemistry [3].

The project has since evolved into a community-building activity and an accessible educational resource. At the 2025 ACS Western Regional Meeting in San Jose, students, chemists, ACS members, and other attendees helped create the tactile table that will be permanently installed at Stanford, while learning about Braille and engaging in conversations about disability, accessibility, and inclusion. [4]

On October 8, this community-created tactile table will find its permanent home in Stanford’s Sapp Center for Science Teaching and Learning where it can continue to educate, spark conversations, and raise awareness about accessibility in science.

Elizabeth Jun
PhD Student, Nuyujukian Lab, Stanford University (profile, lab website)
Elizabeth Jun is a neuroscience PhD Candidate at Stanford University and NIH F31 Predoctoral Fellow funded through National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). Her research interests lie in understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate together to perform computations and support a wide range of behaviors in different contexts. Specifically in her thesis work, advised by Dr. Paul Nuyujukian in the Brain Interfacing Laboratory, she aims to understand how the brain can flexibly support a wide range of complex movements that are supported by a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. She is interested in connecting features of high-dimensional population data to similar behaviors in different contexts, and exploring in general how high-dimensional population features relate back to properties of the neural circuit.
Investigating preserved neural motifs across and within tasks in premotor cortex
Abstract
Motor systems neuroscience studies how populations of motor cortical neurons coordinate to perform motor computations, but less is known about how large repertoires of movements are flexibly generated from a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. There is an emerging idea of conserved neural “modules”, or recurring neural activity patterns deploying computations through dynamics, that may serve as elementary building blocks for performing the same fundamental computation across a wide array of contexts. However, exactly what feature of neural dynamics is “recurring” and fundamentally conserved, if any, when performing the same motor computation within a wide range of reach sequence and kinematic contexts has yet to be shown and characterized empirically.
To investigate this, we trained an animal implanted with a 96-channel Utah array in premotor cortex to perform 4 visually guided arm reaching motor tasks that are composed of unique combinations of 5 distinct motor processes (preparation, initiation, execution, hold, error correction) implemented in various reach conditions, where the same process can reappear across tasks and reappear again within tasks. This design allows us to test the hypothesis that premotor dynamics reuse conserved neural dynamics for performing the same motor computational process, but potentially implemented in different locations and orientations in population state space when reperformed across tasks, repeated in a sequence within tasks, and in different kinematic conditions. In this talk, I will explore systematically testing this hypothesis for all 5 motor processes to understand whether there are general organizing principles for premotor dynamics associated with deploying the same fundamental motor computation in a range of tasks, sequences, and kinematic contexts.

You can also explore recent reviews of Professor Salkin's book by Loren Reinoso, “Salkin, Wendy. Speaking for Others: The Ethics of Informal Political Representation” (Ethics, 2026), and Eline Severs, “Speaking for Others: The Ethics of Informal Political Representation. By Wendy Salkin” (Perspectives on Politics, 2026).

In Speaking for Others: The Ethics of Informal Political Representation, Wendy Salkin provides a novel conceptual and normative theory of informal political representatives, who speak or act for others despite having been neither elected nor selected to do so by means of a systematized election or selection procedure. Informal political representatives are everywhere. Some are internationally recognized leaders of social movements. Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., informally represented Black Montgomerians during the Montgomery Bus Boycott, and Black Americans generally throughout the civil rights movement. Greta Thunberg informally represents Generation Z or, as she has put it, “we who have to live with the consequences” of climate change. Other informal political representatives are just our neighbors and friends. But when they go to the city council meeting to give voice to our neighborhood’s shared interests, they become our representatives too. Despite informal political representatives’ ubiquity and significance to our political lives, their role is conceptually puzzling, morally troubling, and markedly undertheorized. The central ethical challenge of informal political representation is that informal political representatives can provide valuable political goods to those they represent; yet they are neither institutionally nor procedurally constrained in the ways formal political representatives like legislators are. Moreover, informal political representatives are often the only political actors working to advance the interests of oppressed and marginalized groups, meaning these groups rely on their informal political representatives. As a result, relationships between represented groups and informal political representatives can be inegalitarian and oppressive. How may informal political representatives permissibly undertake activities central to their roles without thereby wronging those they represent? This is the question that drives the book.

Wendy Salkin is an Associate Professor of Philosophy and Law at Stanford University, and a Faculty Affiliate at CCSRE. Her research is in political philosophy, philosophy of law, philosophy of race, and Africana philosophy, and intersects with questions in moral philosophy, feminist philosophy, and law. Her book, Speaking for Others: The Ethics of Informal Political Representation (Harvard University Press, 2024) received the Apostolos P. Stefanopoulos Book Prize.

Her research has been generously supported by the American Council of Learned Societies, the Clayman Institute for Gender Research, the ConceptLab, a Laurance S. Rockefeller Visiting Faculty Fellowship at the University Center for Human Values at Princeton University, a Stanford Humanities Seed Grant, and the Stanford Humanities Center.

Salkin received her Ph.D. in Philosophy from Harvard University, her J.D. from Stanford Law School, and her B.A. in Philosophy and Africana Studies from New York University. She has served as a law clerk to the Honorable Judge Rosemary Barkett and the Honorable Judge Adalberto Jordan on the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit in Miami, Florida, and as legal advisor to Judge Barkett on the Iran-United States Claims Tribunal in The Hague.

listings.description:
Abstract:

This lecture investigates the "Buddhist Book Roads," exploring the dynamic transnational spread of Buddhist print culture through a wealth of illustrated books discovered in archaeological sites, statues, and museums. Moving beyond viewing Buddhist woodcuts as static relics, this talk examines their holistic impact within multicultural contexts and as objects transmitted across vast networks both within and beyond Asia. Examples highlight this journey:

The 868 Diamond Sutra from Dunhuang, the world's earliest dated printed book.

Twelfth-to-fourteenth century Lotus Sutra art from Hangzhou, extensively circulated throughout Japan, Korea, and Central Asia.

Printed fragments from Turfan, illuminating elite Uighur migration to Mongol-Yuan China.

The popular 15th-century Beijing Dharani Sutra, sought by female donors for its protective and healing properties.

Moreover, the lecture will demonstrate how Buddhist woodblock images transcended Asian borders, reaching European audiences by the seventeenth century. Four copperplate etchings in a 1670 Dutch travel book, directly copied from Avatamsaka Sutra frontispieces, serve as a prime example. These illustrations mimicked traditional Chinese woodblock prints and calligraphic brushstrokes, shaping European perceptions of Chinese art, religion, and culture.

Bio:

Shih-shan Susan Huang 黃士珊 is the T. T. and W. F. Chao Professor of Transnational Asian Studies at Rice University. Her research explores the intersections of art, religion, and transnational networks in Asia. Her first book, Picturing the True Form: Daoist Visual Culture in Traditional China (Harvard Asia Center, 2012; Chinese translation, Zhejiang University Press, 2022), examines the visual culture of Daoism. Her recent monograph, The Dynamic Spread of Buddhist Print Culture: Mapping Buddhist Book Roads in China and Its Neighbors (Brill, 2024; Chinese edition, forthcoming, Zhejiang University Press), traces how Buddhist texts and images traveled across Asia as dynamic, mobile artifacts. A collection of her scholarly essays, translated into Chinese, is forthcoming from Zhejiang University Press under the title Between Daoism and Buddhism (Daoshi zhijian 道释之间; Zhejiang University Press, forthcoming).

Professor Huang also co-edited Visual and Material Cultures of Middle Period China (Brill, 2017) with the Chinese historian Patricia Ebrey. More recently, she collaborated with the Buddhist scholar Stephen F. Teiser as guest editor of the special issue Ritual and Materiality in Buddhism and Asian Religions in the Hualin International Journal of Buddhist Studies (2025).

She is currently pursuing two new projects: one on the Ten Kings of Hell in Ming–Qing painting and print, and another on the fabrication and reception of Buddhist and Daoist imagery in seventeenth- to nineteenth-century European travel books. Professor Huang held the Hulsewé-Wazniewski Visiting Professorship at Leiden University (the Netherlands) in Spring 2024 and served as Directrice d’études invitée at the École Pratique des Hautes Études, Paris, in Spring 2026.

Trade Policy and Food Security with Climate and Geopolitical Risk

This paper evaluates the effects of trade openness on reliable access to affordable food. We start by showing that the transmission of extreme heat shocks to domestic food prices is weaker in countries with greater trade integration, even conditional on level of development, because productivity shocks are not highly correlated across space. On the other hand, importing countries face disproportionate vulnerability to weather and policy shocks in countries from which they source. We show that global wheat prices diverged in the aftermath of the disruption to Ukrainian exports in 2022, with price increases strongly concentrated in countries importing directly from Ukraine. More broadly, importers face similar effects from extreme heat shocks in source countries, suggesting that global agricultural markets are segmented and countries face adjustment costs to establishing new import sources. We plan to calibrate a quantitative trade model that rationalizes the patterns observed in the data and use it to compare the stability of food prices under varying levels of trade openness, as well as in policy scenarios that specifically subsidize import source diversification.

Bio

Ishan Nath is an Assistant Professor of Public Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School and a Faculty Associate of the Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability. His research focuses broadly on climate change, international trade, and the macroeconomics of development. He currently serves as an associate editor of the Journal of International Economics and the Review of Economics and Statistics. Prior to joining Harvard, Ishan worked as an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and completed postdoctoral fellowships with the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago and in the International Economics section at Princeton University. He received his PhD in Economics from the University of Chicago, an MPhil in Economics from the University of Oxford, and a B.A. in Economics and B.S. in Earth Systems from Stanford University. Curiosity-driven, fundamental research fuels breakthrough technologies and lifesaving therapeutics—with chemistry at the center of it all. Yet, as scientists, we face a critical challenge: public trust in science is at a historic low, and the policy decisions shaping research funding and implementation are evolving rapidly. How do we as researchers bridge the gap between bench science and societal impact?

Join us for an engaging discussion on the interplay among fundamental research, public policy, and national advocacy. Drawing on the history and modern initiatives of the American Chemical Society (ACS), this talk highlights how scientific societies advocate for the research enterprise and how individual researchers can directly influence policy. You will gain insight into the changing landscape of science funding and regulation, as well as concrete tools, fellowships, and advocacy networks designed to help scientists translate their passion for chemical research into real-world policy outcomes.

About the Speaker

Wayne E. Jones Jr. has served as a chemistry faculty member and researcher for 35 years, recently retiring from the University of New Hampshire (UNH). He earned his BS in chemistry from St. Michael’s College in 1987 and his PhD in inorganic chemistry from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1991. Following postdoctoral work at the University of Texas at Austin, he joined the chemistry faculty at the State University of New York (SUNY) at Binghamton, serving in numerous leadership roles for 24 years, including founding director of the Center for Learning and Teaching (1996-2008) and interim dean of Harpur College of Arts and Sciences (2012-2013). He moved to UNH in 2017 to serve as the Dean of Engineering and Physical Sciences, becoming Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs in 2018.

An award winning researcher in inorganic and materials chemistry, he has been recognized as a fellow of the American Chemical Society (2010) and a member of the National Academy of Inventors (2020). He has published over 180 research articles, review chapters and patents in the areas of photoinduced electron and energy transfer in macromolecular systems, including molecular wires, electrically and thermally conducting nanomaterials, photovoltaics in organic/inorganic hybrid materials, photocatalysts for degradation of toxic agents, and fluorescent conjugated polymer sensors with more than 7500 citations. In 2017, he received the SUNY Chancellors Award for Excellence in Research. In 2015, he co-founded Chromananotech LLC, a start up company producing optical nanomaterials patented from his research.

Recipient of several teaching awards, including the SUNY Chancellor’s Award for Excellence in Teaching in 2001, Wayne’s teaching interests focused on long-term curriculum development in chemistry, including more expanded use of technology. He has worked with interdisciplinary teams of scientists and non-scientists on curricular reforms with grant support from the National Science Foundation, Department of Education, and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. In 2008, he established the Go Green Institute, a program designed to inspire middle-school students to pursue careers in science and engineering.

An active volunteer leader in the American Chemical Society for over 30 years, Wayne has served at the local, regional, and national level in ACS leadership roles. He is currently in his third year as Chair of the ACS Board of Directors, and has served as a Director at Large on the Board since 2018. An active leader on several national task forces and committees, he has previously served as chair of the Local Section Activities Committee (LSAC), the Membership Affairs Committee (MAC), and the Committee on Committee’s (CONC), as well as Treasurer of the Northeast Region Board. listings.title: Frances Cayton — Civic Consciousness and the Limits of Attacks on Civil Society
listings.description:
Why do some backsliding incumbents co-opt civil society while others fail? This paper introduces a theory of civic consciousness, contending that, as compared to their formal or political counterparts, informal and apolitical civil society groups often fail to recognize their civic resources. I show that government threats to associational freedom help these groups recognize their latent social capital and increase their willingness to mobilize in support of democracy. As evidence, this paper draws on original data comprising the universe of Polish civil society between 2011 and 2025, a prominent period of democratic erosion and partial recovery. I find that Poland's illiberal PiS government financially targeted formal opposition groups but spared informal, apolitical groups. Meanwhile, those groups developed increased agency, leading them to avoid optional government interactions during the backsliding period. An original civil society-level survey experiment confirms that, when facing government threats, informal and apolitical groups are more likely to engage in pro-democratic actions. Altogether, I illustrate how improved civic consciousness facilitates newfound agency and democratic commitment among previously overlooked corners of civic life.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER

Frances Cayton is the Einstein Moos Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL). Her book project, "How Civic Consciousness Shapes Democratic Resilience," examines how, why, and under what conditions civil society encourages individuals to depolarize and resist democratic erosion. Combining extensive organizational and bureaucratic data, elite and mass surveys, experiments, and interview evidence, she demonstrates how informal and apolitical subsets of civic life retain critical latent democratic potential. More broadly, her research probes the drivers and consequences of democratic engagement, primarily in Eastern Europe while also drawing comparison with other eroding democracies globally. Her research is published or forthcoming in numerous outlets, including the American Journal of Political Science and Perspectives on Politics. Her work has been supported by the US Departments of State and Education, as well as the American Political Science Association.

Cayton holds a PhD in Government from Cornell University. She earned her AM from Harvard University's Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies and a BA from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

listings.title: Directional AI Advice: Experimental Evidence from Healthcare
listings.description:
Generative AI is fast becoming the first-place people turn for expert advice. The advice it provides can be directional rather than neutral, shaped in part by the choices of its designers and regulators. When clients consult AI before meeting an expert, they carry this directional advice into a relationship that once rested on the expert’s judgment alone. We study its consequences in healthcare through a large-scale preregistered field experiment at a Chinese hospital, where we randomize patients’ access to an AI chatbot before their outpatient visit. Examination of the conversation logs shows that the chatbot routinely cautions against the use of medications, especially Traditional Chinese Medicine and antibiotics, while issuing clean recommendations for diagnostic testing, consistent with the liability-driven guardrails encoded in AI training. This directionality propagates into clinical practice. Prescription rates decline among treated patients while diagnostic testing increases, and these effects are more pronounced among physicians who are receptive to patient input and those with more intensive prescribing styles. Beyond shifting healthcare utilization, survey results show that AI access reduces patient compliance and satisfaction, shifting the balance of authority between patients and physicians.

Speaker: Lingsheng Meng is a Senior Research Scholar at the Stanford Center on China’s Economy and Institutions (SCCEI). His research interests are in the fields of labor economics, development economics, and public economics. So far, the bulk of his work is highly empirical and concerned with six main areas: (1) social mobility; (2) inequality; (3) gender disparities; (4) the role of government; (5) political connections; (5) higher education; (6) the US-China trade war. His work appeared in the Journal of Public Economics, the Journal of Human Resources, the Journal of Development Economics, and other peer-reviewed journals. Lingsheng received a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Maryland at College Park in 2010, an M.Phil. in Economics from the Chinese University of Hong Kong in 2004, and a B.A. in Economics and Thai from Peking University in 2002. listings.title: Urban Studies Model Scholar Lecture | How Surprising Neighborhood Changes Are Bringing Down Black-White Segregation
listings.description:
Join Urban Studies for the 20th Annual Model Scholar Lecture featuring John R. Logan, sociology professor at Brown University

About the talk: It is well known by now that the overall level of Black-white segregation in American urban areas is going down. One surprise is that the largest contributions to this decline are coming from predominantly Black neighborhoods that are remaining very disproportionately Black. To a large extent these are the poor inner city neighborhoods that were built up by the Great Migration in the mid-20th Century era of near-apartheid. Their Black residents are leaving them in large numbers and not being replaced by whites or other groups. In itself this exodus is large enough to have a powerful deconcentrating effect. But the second surprise is what is happening in the rest of the metropolis. Neighborhood changes that lower segregation by increasing racial diversity in neighborhoods are outweighed by counter-trends in the opposite direction. Most striking, the positive effect of Black growth in established white neighborhoods -- a new and positive trend, to be sure -- is more than counterbalanced by the continuing Black growth in a different set of Black neighborhoods. If this is the end of a century of segregation, as some have described it, it is arriving with many of the old patterns still in place.

John R. Logan completed his PhD in Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1974. Before coming to Brown he was Distinguished Professor of Sociology and Public Administration at the University at Albany, SUNY; Director of the Mumford Center for Comparative Urban and Regional Research; and Director of the Urban China Research Network. From 2004 through 2016 he served at Brown as Director of the research initiative on Spatial Structures in the Social Sciences. Dr. Logan is co-author, along with Harvey Molotch, of Urban Fortunes: The Political Economy of Place. His most recent edited book, Diversity and Disparities, was published by Russell Sage Foundation in 2015.

About the event: Why do adversaries sometimes cooperate to restrain their military competition? Why do they design arms control agreements with intrusive verification in some cases but rely on minimal transparency in others? Amidst ongoing international competition, arms control remains rare despite potential mutual benefits, and agreements vary dramatically in their approaches to monitoring. This book reveals how uncertainty from domestic political changes - such as leadership transitions or social unrest - can enable arms control. It identifies two paths to agreement: during periods of uncertainty, states that previously relied on informal understandings hedge by establishing lightly-monitored agreements, while those that anticipated deception take calculated risks through agreements with intensive verification. Through comprehensive data analysis and rich case studies, Jane Vaynman challenges conventional wisdom about uncertainty in international relations while offering insights for policymakers. As states confront challenges from nuclear competition to emerging technologies, understanding when arms control becomes viable is more vital than ever.

About the speaker: Dr. Jane Vaynman is an Assistant Professor of Strategic Studies at the School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS) at Johns Hopkins University. Dr. Vaynman’s work focuses on security cooperation between adversarial states, the design of arms control agreements, and the effects of technology on patterns of international cooperation and competition. From 2022-2024, she served as a senior advisor in the Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence, and Stability at the U.S. Department of State. Her prior academic appointments include the Department of Political Science at Temple University and the Elliott School of International Affairs, George Washington University. She was also previously a Lightning Scholar at Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania, a Stanton Nuclear Security Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, and a Fulbright Fellow at the Carnegie Moscow Center. Florida has long been a laboratory for the policing and confinement of noncitizens. This talk asks how the war on migrants is spatialized in the suburb. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork on the agricultural peripheries of Miami, it engages unregulated informal housing and “alternative to detention” surveillance. Migrant agricultural workers in South Miami-Dade often live in trailers, efficiencies, sheds, and auto-constructed structures without formal addresses. Without access to an address, tenants cannot enroll children in school, comply with asylum requirements, or contest unjust eviction. Many of these migrant tenants also participate in the Intensive Surveillance Appearance Program, a federal “alternative to detention program” that tracks and conditions migrant mobility. These diffuse and dispersed forms of spatial containment produce cascading social and political foreclosures for migrant tenant-workers. This talk develops the analytic of the “periphery within” to illuminate a suburban geography of dispossession that operates not through confinement or disappearance but through the private and parceled proliferation of the labor camp.

Emma Shaw Crane is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Anthropology at Stanford University. She is an ethnographer of war and environment in the Americas. Her current book project, Counterinsurgent Suburb, draws on fieldwork on and surrounding a military base and detention camp for migrant children in South Florida to investigate the environmental and spatial relationships that sustain U.S. war-making. Emma received her PhD in American Studies from New York University and was a postdoctoral fellow in the Society of Fellows at Columbia University, where she was affiliated with the Center for the Study of Ethnicity and Race. Futuring Black Lives is a historical ethnography examining Black institution builders in the late 1960s and early 1970s and their work to leverage the power of publications and the literary imagination to engage “concerned men and women” in conversations about the educational journeys and futures of Black children. While many began as reactions to anti-Blackness and American public schooling failing Black children, Independent Black Institutions (IBIs) came to be viable ecosystems anchored in a shared Black value system preparing Black children in three areas: identity, purpose, and direction.

The rationale for establishing and valuing IBIs remains highly relevant, given the sociopolitical landscape of education today. In addition to persistent racial disparities in academic achievement and Black students’ highly disproportionate experiences of punishment and “discipline,” friction and legislation against critical examination of race, racism, and racist ideas in school settings are front and center, and children’s and young adult literature are under attack through censorship and outright book bans. Yet Black institution builders left useful maps of and for the educational future/s of Black children that remain available in journals, newspapers, pamphlets, and other ephemera. Author Maisha T. Winn demonstrates how and why the historiography-grounded futuring of Black education can and should inform current pursuits of equity, justice, and liberation through education.

Maisha T. Winn is the Excellence in Learning Graduate School of Education Professor and Faculty Director of the Stanford Accelerator for Learning's Equity in Learning Initiative. She is the Principal Investigator for the Futuring for Equity Lab. Her scholarship examines how non-dominant youth and communities have developed literate trajectories across a range of historical and contemporary settings within and outside formal schooling. She seeks to understand how communities that have been depicted as under resourced create practices, processes, and institutions of their own—and what we can learn from those examples to build more just, more collaborative, and more equitable futures. An ethnographer by training, Dr. Winn also engages in historical research focused on social movements in education.

listings.title: Nicholas Branigan | Non-ergodicity and Simpson’s paradox in neural correlates
listings.description:
Abstract

What are the neural correlates of human behavior? Much research has approached versions of this question between individuals but not within individuals (over time). Are results from these 2 approaches similar? To address this, we mapped the neural correlates of 4 cognitive measures both between and within individuals in over 4000 people. We combined fMRI with a probabilistic model of the stop signal task that we developed to capture trial-level variation in cognitive measures. For each of these measures, neural correlates diverged between versus within individuals—a striking example of non-ergodicity and Simpson’s paradox. For example, individuals with worse control had less brain activity, but when an individual had worse control they had more brain activity. I’ll argue that non-ergodicity creates both challenges and opportunities for human neuroscience. Studies relying on individual-average measures have left unanswered fundamental questions about temporal dynamics. This means that our picture of the neural correlates of cognition and disease may be dramatically incomplete, but it also suggests that new discoveries could come from experiments and models that now target within-individual variation.

Bio

Nicholas is a Research Data Analyst at Stanford with Vinod Menon. He is interested in developing methods to understand large-scale behavioral and brain data. He has worked on developing probabilistic machine learning models, including drift-diffusion models of cognitive control and state-space models of fMRI and calcium imaging. Before falling for neuroscience, Nicholas worked in experimental economics with Muriel Niederle and philanthropic strategy with Paul Brest. He received an MS in statistics and a BA in economics, both from Stanford.

About the Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series

The Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series is a platform for trainees across campus to share insights and innovative approaches that bridge the gap between neuroscience and data science.

As neuroscience continues to generate vast amounts of data—from intricate neural circuit maps to large-scale brain activity recordings—the need for interdisciplinary expertise in data science, statistics, and engineering has never been more critical.

listings.title: Elamite Art Through the Lens of Archaeological Evidence
listings.description:
Event is in Persian.

Professor Bahram Ghadiri examines Elamite art as a major body of archaeological evidence for understanding the cultural, political, and religious development of southwestern Iran and the broader Iranian Plateau. Rather than approaching Elamite art primarily as a collection of isolated aesthetic objects, the presentation situates artistic production within its historical, geographical, and social contexts.

The lecture begins with an overview of the emergence of Elamite political formations and their changing territorial extent from the late fourth millennium to the first millennium BCE. It considers the relationships among important centers such as Susa, Anshan, Haft Tappeh, Chogha Zanbil, and the highland regions associated with Elamite cultural traditions.

The second section addresses the principal methodological challenges involved in interpreting Elamite art. Particular attention is given to archaeological context, chronology, iconography, inscriptions, patterns of cultural exchange, and the limitations created by incomplete or displaced evidence. The lecture also considers how earlier scholarly frameworks have influenced modern interpretations of Elamite artistic identity.

The final section examines selected examples of monumental architecture, rock reliefs, seals, sculpture, metalwork, ceramics, and representations of music and ritual. These materials illuminate concepts of kingship, religious practice, social organization, collective memory, and interaction with Mesopotamia and neighboring regions.

By integrating artistic analysis with archaeological evidence, the lecture presents Elamite civilization as a dynamic and internally diverse cultural tradition. It further explores Elam’s significant contribution to the long-term cultural development of ancient Iran while avoiding the projection of modern national identities onto ancient societies.

Bahram Ghadiri was born in 1949 in Tehran, Iran. He graduated from Tehran University, where he studied under noted philosophers on Islamic and Persian art and architecture such as Titus Burkhardt, Henry Corbin and Hossein Nasr. His interest in the traditional art and architecture led him to engage in practical learning with master-masons and artists. At the age of 28 he became the Director of Niyavaran National Cultural Center, one of the most prestigious centers for art and architecture in Iran. Among his many projects in Iran are the restoration and revitalization of Akhavan Sigari Mansion (Yazd), Tajrish Municipal Libraries (Tehran), Main Entrance Gate to Bazaar Shishegar Khaneh (Tabriz), Seyed Aladin Hossein Mausoleum (a village near Hamadan), Miandasht Caravansary Complex (Miandasht on Silkroad), Dar Al-fonun School (Tehran), and Khan Bathhouse (Yazd Bazaar). In 2001, the Khan Bathhouse was the winner of the Aga Khan Foundation Award for Architecture prize. As a professor of Historic Preservation in the School of Architecture & Urban Planning, Shahid Beheshti University from 1986 to 2003, Professor Ghadiri led 16 years of research on Persian bazaars, a first of its kind in the nation, involving over 800 graduate students. The result was a complete survey of the physical and non-physical elements, and developing a methodology for study of bazaars and their causes of decay. He also served as visiting professor at the School of Architecture & Urban Planning at Yazd University and Isfahan University (1995-2001). Professor Ghadiri is the author of four books, 30 articles and over a half a dozen academic handouts on topics of conservation and preservation of Iranian historical building, city fabric, and bazaars. He is also the founder and president of Foundation for Persian Archaeological Studies.

listings.title: Paweł Adamowicz and the Civic Ethos of Inclusion: Urban Democracy After the Assassination
listings.description:
The 2019 assassination of Paweł Adamowicz, Mayor of Gdańsk, marked a decisive moment in Poland’s political trajectory, revealing how anti immigrant rhetoric can harden into physical violence. This talk examines Adamowicz’s death as the culmination of a sustained campaign against pro integration politics – a campaign directed at him precisely because he advanced a vision of national belonging rooted in civic openness rather than ethnonationalism.

Adamowicz’s integration agenda drew on Christian social teaching, including papal messages on migration and the Catholic principles embedded in Gdańsk’s Immigrant Integration Model. His approach aligned with Benjamin Barber’s conviction that cities, rather than nation states, function as democratic bulwarks: pragmatic, diverse, and dependent on newcomers for social and economic vitality. For Barber, immigrants do not threaten urban cohesion; they generate it, bringing skills, energy, and civic potential that strengthen cities’ capacity to innovate and govern. Adamowicz’s Christian inflected urban pluralism — grounded in hospitality, dignity, and shared responsibility — thus stood in stark contrast to Poland’s rising illiberal currents.

This pluralism extended beyond migration. Adamowicz championed LGBTQ+ inclusion through initiatives such as the Model for Equal Treatment, municipal anti discrimination programs, and public support for Gdańsk’s Equality March. These policies articulated a broader ethics of belonging: a city that protects its minorities protects its democratic future. Figures such as Karol Nawrocki (today serving as President of Poland) publicly attacked him, claiming that he was “a politician who does not recognize what is sacred,” a charge that inverted Adamowicz’s own reliance on Catholic doctrine to defend inclusion.

Yet the aftermath of the assassination revealed a different trajectory than the one intended by his attackers. Instead of producing civic chaos or deepening polarization, Adamowicz’s death generated an unprecedented public outpouring of grief and solidarity. In Gdańsk, tens of thousands mobilized around the very principles he had championed — openness, equality, and the protection of newcomers — reaffirming inclusion as the city’s guiding civic ethos. In the years since, Gdańsk has continued to develop policies rooted in this ethic, demonstrating how urban governance can transform trauma into a renewed commitment to democratic pluralism.

This talk argues that Adamowicz’s legacy lies not only in the threats he faced, but in the inclusive civic imagination that survived him: a model of urban democracy in which cities respond to violence not with fear, but with deeper solidarity and an expanded sense of who belongs.

Izabela Morska is a Polish scholar and writer, Professor of English and American Studies at the University of Gdańsk. Her current research on Paweł Adamowicz examines civic ethics, pluralism, and the cultural imaginaries of democracy. She holds an MA from the University of Gdańsk, a PhD from the Polish Academy of Sciences, and an MFA from Mills College, and has held research appointments at the University College Dublin Humanities Institute, the Open Society Archives at CEU Budapest, the Russian Institute for Advanced Study in Moscow, and the Beatrice Bain Research Group at UC Berkeley. A recipient of the Polish Ministry of Culture scholarship for The Legacy of Paweł Adamowicz project, she works at the intersection of media studies, border studies, and narrative ethics. listings.title: The Fate of the Social in Modern Life: American Social Scientists and Japan as Archive
listings.description:
In the decades following World War II, American social scientists turned to the study of Japanese society as an emerging ally and fellow capitalist democracy. At a time when influential theories of modernization predicted the decline of kinship, community, hierarchy, and collective obligation, Japan presented a puzzle. It was an advanced industrial and capitalist society in which village, family, corporate welfare, and moral persuasion in public institutions played powerful roles in organizing everyday life.

This talk examines how postwar scholars treated Japan not simply as an object of study but as a site for thinking through a larger problem in modern social thought: the relationship between individual freedom and social solidarity. Drawing on chapters from a larger book project, I revisit three influential studies of Japan: Ruth Benedict's The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946), Ezra Vogel's Japan's New Middle Class (1963), and Thomas Rohlen's For Harmony and Strength (1974). I argue that these works are best understood not only as interpretations of Japan but also as reflections on what I call the "social question" in postwar thought: how modern societies cultivate attachment, obligation, welfare, and collective purpose while preserving democratic freedoms and individual autonomy. By placing these texts in conversation, the talk suggests that postwar Japan functioned as a distinctive archive for thinking about enduring questions of social reproduction and social solidarity in democratic life.

Amy Borovoy is a cultural anthropologist and professor in the Department of East Asian Studies at Princeton University. Her book, The Too-Good Wife (2005), explored heavy drinking in Japan and its effects on the wives who must cope with their husbands’ alcoholism. She has also written on social withdrawal, public health and mass screening, and Covid-19 containment in Japan. Her manuscript in progress, In Search of Social Solidarity, explores how American social scientists after World War II made sense of postwar Japan not simply as an object of study but as a site for thinking through a larger problem in modern social thought: the relationship between individual autonomy and social solidarity, community welfare, and the socialization of the self.

Presented by the Department of Art & Art History, this art history lightning talk event features three distinguished alums—Altair Brandon-Salmon, Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz, and Sabrina Buell. Each alum will give a 15-minute presentation on their work and area of expertise, followed by a brief 5-minute discussion. The event will be moderated by Head Librarian Lindsay King.

EVENT PROGRAM

Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail

Speaker: Altair Brandon-Salmon (PhD ’24)

In 1938, the National Gallery in London published One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery, written by its young director, Kenneth Clark (1903-83). Old Master paintings in the collection were presented as cropped, black-and-white pairs. The book, with its witty commentary and beautiful production, was a huge success.

This curator’s talk will illuminate the Bowes Art and Architecture Library’s exhibition Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail, which is the first to take One Hundred Details as the lynchpin to understand how details—cropped reproductions of paintings—were central to looking at art in the early 20th century. From the groundbreaking work of art historians to avant-garde publications, the exhibition shows that these monochrome details, published facing one another across a page spread, created a distinctive, modernist way of seeing Old Master painting.

Altair Brandon-Salmon is an art historian and a lecturer in Civic, Liberal, and Global Education at Stanford University. His scholarship on modern art has appeared in Art History, Art Journal, British Art Studies, and the Oxford Art Journal. He has been a curator for the Sheldonian Theatre and Campion Hall, University of Oxford, and he is currently a guest curator for Projects Twenty Two. His book, Rubble: Art, the Blitz, and London in Ruins, is forthcoming in spring 2027.

Setting Art Up For Success: A Career in Art Conservation

Speaker: Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz (BA ‘04)

Art Conservators often think about how their actions will impact artworks many years from now. Throughout her career in art conservation and museum administration, Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz (‘04) has brought this long-term perspective to the conservation of individual artworks, public art installations, and museum administration. This talk will look at how considering the long-term interaction of art-making materials, conservation choices, and exhibition sites can strengthen the preservation and maintenance of artworks, particularly in public installations and private collections.

Alisa Eagleston-Cieslewicz holds a MA in art history with an advanced certificate in art conservation from the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University and an MBA from the Haas School of Business at UC Berkeley. She has held positions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, SFO Museum, and The Foster Museum. She is currently an objects conservator and museum consultant in private practice at Mayfield Art Conservation and Consulting LLC, where she works with museums and collectors to conserve their artworks and to build the institutional infrastructure to support ongoing collections care. Alisa also serves on the Historic Resources Board for the City of Palo Alto and on the board of the Bay Area Art Conservation Guild.

Building a Collection: the Eye, the Market, and Public Art at Stanford

Speaker: Sabrina Buell (BA ’99)

Sabrina Buell will trace her path at the intersection of art and business, from studying Art History and Economics at Stanford through her 25 years in the business as an Advisor to many of the most important public and private collections of our time. Chief among the public collections she and her firm have advised is Stanford University. She will speak about the growing public art collection on campus, the Denning House collection for the Knight-Hennessy scholars, and Stanford’s commitment to the arts on campus going forward.

Sabrina Buell founded Zlot Buell + Associates, a cross-generational, multifaceted art advisory firm, in 2012. She was previously a Director at Matthew Marks Gallery in New York for 10 years. Sabrina grew up in San Francisco and holds degrees from Stanford University and NYU.

listings.title: Two Views of the Chinese Coast
listings.description:
Join us for "Two Views of the Chinese Coast," a talk by Kären Wigen, the Frances & Charles Field Professor in Stanford's Department of History, at the David Rumsey Map Center. When cartographic collections began to appear online in the 1990s, historians of East Asia were quick to seize on maps as subjects for research. Over the next thirty years, a sophisticated field of critical map studies developed, illuminating the lively landscape of cartographic production across the early modern Sinosphere. While map-focused research made rapid strides, a gap gradually opened between cartographic research (the history of maps) and what we might call map-informed history (history with maps).

This talk attempts to address that gap by investigating two works from Stanford University Libraries’ collections: a Qing-era scroll painting of the Pacific coast, housed in the David Rumsey Map Collection, and a British map of the same shoreline from 1859, owned by a private collector and held digitally within the Barry Lawrence Ruderman Map Collection. During the 19th century, both maps served as tools of military planning; where the Qing scroll was likely consulted for coastal defense, the British chart was designed for a naval attack. By putting them in dialogue with each other, the talk suggests how cross-cultural map comparison can help us tell more complex, entangled stories about Euro-Asian interaction.

Speaker Bio

Kären Wigen teaches Japanese history and the history of cartography. A geographer by training, she earned her doctorate at the University of California at Berkeley. Her first book, The Making of a Japanese Periphery, 1750-1920 (1995), mapped the economic transformation of southern Nagano Prefecture during the heyday of the silk industry. Her second book, A Malleable Map: Geographies of Restoration in Central Japan, 1600-1912 (2010), returned to the ground of that study, exploring the roles of cartography, chorography, and regionalism in the making of modern Shinano. An abiding interest in world history led her to co-author The Myth of Continents (1997) with Martin Lewis. She also introduced a forum on oceans in history for the American Historical Review and co-edited Seascapes: Maritime Histories, Littoral Cultures, and Transoceanic Exchanges (2007) with Jerry Bentley and Renate Bridenthal. Her latest book is Territorial Imaginaries: Beyond the Sovereign Map (2025).

listings.description:
The High Cost of Extreme Weather Under Climate Change

Climate change is already altering the frequency and intensity of weather extremes, with large and growing costs around the world. However, considering only realized losses understates the costs of climate-change driven extremes because it misses the substantial costs of preparing for and managing disaster risk. Climate change can greatly increase these costs by rendering past experience of weather potentially unrepresentative of current exposure, greatly increasing uncertainty in the extreme tail of the climate distribution. Here we quantify these ambiguity-related costs for urban flood damages in the United States. Using daily rainfall for 151 US cities from 1970 to 2024, we contrast the 2024 extreme rainfall distribution under a Bayesian model that assumes a stationary rainfall distribution with one that allows for time-evolving Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) parameters. Estimated tail-risks increase notably under a time-varying climate and are amplified by convex damage functions, which we estimate at the city level using flood insurance policy and claim data. The 99th percentile loss event - a regulatory standard for financial risk management - is 4-5 times larger under time-varying climate risk at all levels of geographic diversification, implying much larger capital holding requirements and insurance supply costs in a private market. We show that most (66%) of this effect comes from additional ambiguity in a time-varying climate, rather than correcting bias in the central estimate. Findings have important implications for the sustainability of private insurance markets in a changing climate and the government role in managing catastrophic climate risk.

Bio

Frances C. Moore is Professor and Hurlston Presidential Chair in the Environmental Science and Policy Department at the University of California Davis. Her work focuses on better understanding the social and economic costs of climate change, with applications to mitigation and adaptation policy. Her research encompasses a range of applied and theoretical problems at the intersection of climate science and environmental economics including estimating the social cost of carbon, the welfare consequences of climate impacts on natural capital, insurance and the management of catastrophic risk, and the value of climate information for adaptation and resilience decisions. In 2026-27, Fran is serving as the Policy Fellow at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University where she is advancing modeling of the coupled climate-social system. In 2022-23 she served in the Biden Administration as the Senior Economist at the Council of Economic Advisers covering climate, clean energy and environmental issues.

Climate Change and Counteradaptation

Mainstream climate research and policy often treat adaptation as a neutral, technical process, favoring top-down "adjustment" approaches. This seminar argues that these paradigms obscure how vulnerability in the Global South is actively produced by colonial dispossession, racial capitalism, and illicit financial flows—ultimately pushing communities to adjust to unjust structures rather than transform them. Borrowing from evolutionary biology, where counteradaptation describes traits that evolve in antagonistic response to another organism's adaptations or behavior, this seminar proposes counteradaptation as a critical analytic lens. This framework reveals that communities are largely adapting not to geophysical forces, but to colonial legacies and the social structures that sustain them. Ultimately, reframing climate response as counteradaptation shifts the focus from passive resilience toward the necessity of reparative transformation.

Bio: Eugene Richardson, MD, PhD, is a physician-anthropologist in the Department of Global Health and Social Medicine at Harvard Medical School, where he directs the Paul Farmer Planetary Health Lab. His research examines vulnerability to epidemics and climate change, and from that work he has developed a new theory of counteradaptation, which he will present at this seminar.

What can a whale, a dumpling, and an endangered clouded leopard tell us about belonging?

Join artist and designer Yiying Lu, creator of Twitter’s Fail Whale and six emoji adopted into the Unicode Standard, for an opening talk celebrating Wild & Bright, an exhibition of nine large-scale digital paintings from her multi-year series on endangered species, on view in Hohbach Hall at Green Library through 2028.

Lu will trace the unexpected creative path connecting these seemingly different worlds: from a personal illustration that became Twitter’s Fail Whale in 2008, to emoji designed to expand the world’s shared visual vocabulary, to a red panda created for a Bay Area AAPI night market that opened an entirely new direction in her practice.

That exploration eventually led Lu to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, where her logo design for COP15 received an Award of Honor, and to support from the Adobe Creative Residency Community Fund. Wild & Bright began on August 4, 2020, International Clouded Leopard Day, with the clouded leopard as the first animal in the series.

The work has since returned to the community in new ways. In 2025, sixteen pieces from the series were featured at a San Francisco Zoo fundraising gala, bringing art, storytelling, and wildlife conservation together.

Across Lu’s work runs a central question:

What does it take to make someone, or something, feel like it belongs in the picture?

She approaches belonging as a design inquiry: whether the subject is a species losing its natural habitat, a culture missing from a global visual language, or a whale that made failure feel unexpectedly human.
